def: An agreement between the sides in a conflict to stop fighting, for a set time or while talks go on. It does not by itself end a war.
Acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group. It is defined in the 1948 UN Genocide Convention, and courts decide whether it has happened.
A serious crime, such as murder, torture or forced displacement, committed as part of a widespread or systematic attack on civilians.
A serious breach of the laws of war, such as deliberately attacking civilians or mistreating prisoners.
A panel of independent experts set up, for example by the UN Human Rights Council, to investigate alleged abuses and report what it finds. It is not a court.
An ordinary aerial bomb fitted with folding wings and guidance, so a plane can release it many kilometres from its target.
Using military force to stop ships or goods from reaching or leaving a country's ports or borders.
An explosive placed in the water that goes off when a ship touches it or passes close to it.
The narrow sea passage between Iran and Oman that links the Persian Gulf to the open ocean. A large share of the world's oil and gas exports pass through it.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a powerful military force separate from the regular army that answers to the Supreme Leader.
US Central Command, the part of the US military responsible for the Middle East and parts of Central and South Asia.
US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, for all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and about a third of the Senate.
The US national legislature. It has two chambers, the House of Representatives and the Senate, and both must pass a bill before the president can sign it into law.
A formal process in which a legislature charges a senior official, such as a president, with misconduct and can vote to remove them from office.
A leader's power to reject a law passed by the legislature. In the US, Congress can override a veto with a two-thirds vote in both chambers.
The rate a central bank sets for lending to banks. Raising it makes borrowing more expensive, which usually slows spending and inflation.
The rate at which prices rise over time. It is often measured by the consumer price index (CPI), a basket of everyday goods and services.
A takeover in which the buyer pays with its own shares instead of cash, so the target's shareholders become shareholders of the buyer.
A measure of what a whole company is worth: the value of its shares plus its debt, minus its cash.
A severe, often deadly disease caused by a group of viruses and spread through contact with the body fluids of an infected person. Bundibugyo and Zaire are two different strains.
A study in people that tests whether a medicine or vaccine is safe and whether it works.
A natural warming of the surface of the tropical Pacific Ocean every few years. It shifts weather around the world and tends to push global temperatures up.
The average global temperature in 1850-1900, the baseline scientists use to measure how much the planet has warmed.
The aim, set in the 2015 Paris Agreement, of limiting long-term global warming to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels. It refers to an average over many years, not a single year.
All the frozen parts of Earth: glaciers, ice sheets, sea ice, snow and permanently frozen ground (permafrost).
Time an astronaut spends working outside a spacecraft in a spacesuit. NASA calls it extravehicular activity (EVA).
An attempt to break into, damage or take control of computers, networks or connected devices.
The basic software built into a device, such as a fridge controller or router, that tells its hardware what to do. Fixes are installed as firmware updates.
Violence or threats against people, used to frighten the public or push a political or ideological goal. Each country's law defines it a little differently.
Three goals, or in rugby three tries, scored by one player in a single match.
Europe's top club football competition, run each season by UEFA.
Money earned from cinema ticket sales. Weekend figures are first released as studio estimates and later updated.
